hints: Start by looking at the large-scale organisation - how many separate cytoplasmic areas divided by a wall can you see inside the outer mother cell?
Now count the dark-stained clusters of chromosomes - how many distinct groups are moving, and how many groups are there in each compartment?
Look at the shape and position of the chromosomes - are they lined up in the middle, or are they stretched out and moving toward opposite ends with V-shapes?
Think about what must be attached to the chromosomes to move them, and what happens to the nuclear envelope during this type of stage.
Link the two observations together - two cells each dividing again means the first division is finished, so which division and which phase of that division fits best?
walkthrough:
Reading What You Can Actually See**
You are looking at one original plant mother cell, but inside it there are already two separate cells divided by a curved wall. That tells you the first meiotic division has finished. Inside those two cells you can see four dark groups of chromosomes in total, two groups in each cell.

Why This Must Be Meiosis II**
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes and produces two haploid cells. Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids in both of those cells at the same time, just like mitosis. Seeing two cells dividing simultaneously is the classic signature of meiosis II, not meiosis I.

Why This Is Anaphase**
In metaphase the chromosomes would be lined up in a neat row on the equator. Here they are not. They are in groups moving apart toward opposite ends, stretched into V-shapes. That movement apart is anaphase. Because it is happening in both meiosis II cells, it is anaphase II.

How The Movement Happens**
Each chromatid has a centromere with a kinetochore where spindle fibres made of microtubules attach. The spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids apart, now called daughter chromosomes, to opposite poles. The centromere is pulled first so it leads, with the chromosome arms trailing behind. There is no nuclear envelope around the chromosomes during this active movement.

Final answer: Anaphase II of meiosis II; two cells visible following meiosis I with four groups of chromosomes in total, two groups per cell; sister chromatids / daughter chromosomes being pulled to opposite poles by shortening spindle fibres / microtubules attached to centromeres / kinetochores; centromeres lead with arms trailing; no nuclear envelope visible.
